analysis.one_liner: Makes nuclear contractors repay the government if their gross negligence or willful misconduct causes accident liability.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring Department of Energy nuclear contractors to repay the government for liability caused by gross negligence or willful misconduct drew 50 cosponsors but died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a nuclear accident happens at a facility run by a private contractor for the Department of Energy, the federal government pays the public liability claims under the Price-Anderson indemnification system — even if the accident was the contractor's own fault. This bill would change that: the Justice Department could sue to claw back those payments from a contractor whose gross negligence or willful misconduct caused the harm, the contractor could not be quietly reimbursed by the Energy Department, and a contractor found liable would be barred from new federal contracts for five years. The bill never got out of committee and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently foot the bill for public liability claims even when a nuclear contractor's own gross negligence or willful misconduct caused the harm; and people living near nuclear facilities, who would gain a financial accountability backstop. The bill would not change compensation available to accident victims — it changes who ultimately bears the cost when the government pays on a contractor's behalf.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near nuclear sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets the Attorney General sue a DOE contractor, subcontractor, or supplier to recover any indemnification payments the federal government made for public liability resulting from the contractor's gross negligence or willful misconduct.
It closes a loophole by barring the Department of Energy from reimbursing — directly or indirectly — any amount recovered from a contractor.
A contractor from whom money is recovered would be ineligible for any federal contract for five years, with a presidential exemption only to protect national security.
Recovery is capped at the contract price the contractor received for the work that gave rise to the liability, limiting the penalty to what the contractor earned from the activity.

analysis.who_pays: DOE nuclear contractors and their subcontractors and suppliers, who would face repayment of government indemnity payments capped at their contract price, possible five-year debarment from federal contracts, and renegotiated compensation terms if they request them.

drawbacks.text: DOE contractors perform hazardous nuclear work largely because the liability risks are otherwise uninsurable; a clawback plus debarment regime could make contractors refuse the work, demand higher pay, or raise costs for the government's nuclear cleanup and defense programs.
The recovery is capped at the total contract price for the year the work was performed, so the government could still recover far less than the full cost of a serious accident it paid for.
The five-year federal contracting ban includes a presidential national-security exemption, which could allow a debarred contractor essential to defense programs to keep its contracts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is straightforward: shifting the cost of contractor-caused nuclear liability from taxpayers to the contractors themselves, bounded by what the contractor earned from the work. The honest objection is that indemnification exists because nuclear liability is a risk the private market will not insure; making contractors face clawbacks and debarment could raise the price of nuclear cleanup and defense contracting or dry up willing contractors. The bill's design partially acknowledges this with a contract-price cap and a national-security exemption, but it never advanced far enough for those balances to be tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House committee and then to a subcommittee, sat there for the rest of the Congress, and died when the session ended without a hearing vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller introduced the Price-Anderson Financial Accountability Amendments on February 23, 1989, with 30 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs, and on March 17, 1989, to its Subcommittee on Energy and the Environment.
The bill attracted 50 cosponsors — 45 House Democrats and 5 House Republicans.
No further action was taken; the bill never left the subcommittee and never received a vote in either chamber before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: DOE nuclear contractors and their suppliers came out ahead: the existing system stayed in place, under which the federal government pays public liability claims for nuclear accidents and does not claw the money back from contractors whose gross negligence or willful misconduct caused the harm.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make DOE contractors financially accountable for liability caused by gross negligence or willful misconduct.

for.name: 45 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Waxman, Pelosi, Markey, Stark, Wyden, and DeFazio among the original group.

for.name: 5 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small share of Republican support.

against.name: House Interior and Insular Affairs Subcommittee on Energy and the Environment
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 17, 1989, and never reported it out; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Morris Udall
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, presided over a panel that never advanced the bill past its subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was mostly Democratic (45 of 257 Democrats cosponsored) but included 5 of 175 Republicans, and no chamber ever voted, so party lines on the merits were never tested.

industries.industry: DOE nuclear contractors and their suppliers
industries.note: The bill would have required them to repay federal indemnity payments when their own gross negligence or willful misconduct causes public liability, barred DOE from reimbursing them, and barred them from federal contracts for five years. Today the government — meaning taxpayers — absorbs that cost.

industries.industry: Government contracting for nuclear facility operations
industries.note: Clawbacks and debarment could push contractors to charge more or avoid hazardous DOE work, raising the cost of nuclear cleanup and defense programs; the national-security exemption was designed to keep essential contractors available.
